text:
A US court found Google’s search business a monopoly because the company engaged in exclusionary conduct by paying billions of dollars to be set as the default search engine, creating a self-reinforcing loop where defaults lead to scale, data, and quality that protect its market position. Judge Amit Mehta ruled on August 5, 2024 [Source: ev-1], that Google violated Section 2 of the Sherman Act through these default-distribution deals with partners like Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla. Evidence showed Google paid approximately $26.3 billion for distribution in 2021 and gave Apple roughly 36% of Safari search-ad revenue [Source: ev-1].

The remedies ordered on August 5, 2 conduct were structural: Google must sell Chrome (the first forced divestiture of a major tech company since the Microsoft case of 2000), may no longer pay for default search placement via revenue-sharing agreements, and faces limits on acquisitions and AI-related investments [Source: ev-1].
